summary:
I developed a rule-based health-monitoring framework for astronauts. It tracks daily readings such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, oxygen, balance, bone density, exercise, sleep, temperature, and mood. Each reading is classified as Normal, Below normal, Above normal, or Critical, and each class has a set action: log it, recheck and find the cause, or stop and call the medical officer.

A mental health monitor combines mood check-ins with sleep, heart rate, and fatigue trends to spot stress, isolation, and burnout early. A mind game, using short reaction-time and memory tasks, helps the crew relax while checking alertness and consciousness against each astronaut's own baseline. A drop triggers the same response steps.

The challenge is that space changes the body and mind. Bone loss, balance problems, and shifts in heart rate and blood pressure mean Earth ranges don't always apply, and doctors are far away. The crew needs clear first steps without waiting for Earth. The system stays safe: it never diagnoses or chooses medication, it only triggers first aid and refers everything else to the medical officer.

This matters because it catches problems early, gives fast, consistent responses in remote conditions, and protects the whole crew, since one sick, exhausted, or overloaded astronaut risks the mission. It also tracks long-term trends like bone loss, sleep, and mental wellbeing, essential for missions to the Moon and Mars.
details:
What it does: A wrist wearable tracks heart rate (MAX30102) and cabin pressure, temperature and altitude (BMP390). Every second it calculates a health score, a fatigue index and a risk level: Normal, Above or Critical. It then sends the results as JSON over Bluetooth Low Energy to a phone or ground station, with a plain-language recommendation such as "Rest 15 min" or "Notify flight surgeon immediately."

Benefits:

• Continuous, non-invasive monitoring with no manual checks.

• Early warning of fatigue, abnormal heart rate or hypoxia.

• Clear recommendations the crew can act on, even when contact with Earth is delayed.

• Mental health monitor: tracks stress and mood signs such as heart-rate changes and fatigue trends, and flags when a crew member may need rest or support.

• Mind game: short, engaging brain games that help crew members relax, stay sharp and fight isolation and boredom. They can also show how focus and reaction time change over a mission.

• Low-cost, low-power, wireless hardware.

Intended impact: Safer, more independent crews on long missions, with physical and mental health visible in one place. The same design can help climbers, remote workers and first responders.

Tools: C++ (Arduino IDE), nRF52 BLE board, MAX30102, BMP390, I²C, BLE and JSON.

Creativity: It combines body and environment sensing with a mission-themed "digital flight surgeon," and it treats mental wellbeing as seriously as physical health.

Factors considered: safety thresholds, reliable sensor readings, low power, a small size and easy expansion.
